description: Little Rock Nine, the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the rise of Martin Luther King Jr 1954–1960.
content_html:
Resistance to Brown and the Little Rock Crisis

The Supreme Court’s Brown ruling of 1954 did not automatically desegregate American schools. The follow-up ruling, Brown II (1955), only required desegregation to proceed with “all deliberate speed” — a phrase Southern states exploited to delay. The most dramatic confrontation came in September 1957 at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Nine Black students, later known as the Little Rock Nine, attempted to enrol. Governor Orval Faubus called out the National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower, though personally reluctant to intervene, could not allow a state governor to defy a federal court order. He sent 1,000 soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students inside.

Key Fact

In September 1957, nine Black students tried to enter Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Governor Faubus used the National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to escort them in — the first use of federal troops to enforce civil rights in the South since Reconstruction.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott 1955–1956

On 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a segregated Montgomery, Alabama bus and was arrested. She was not simply a tired seamstress — Parks was a trained NAACP activist who had attended civil rights workshops at the Highlander Folk School. Her arrest was chosen by the NAACP as a legal test case precisely because Parks was an ideal plaintiff: dignified, educated and without a compromising personal history.

The Black community of Montgomery responded with a boycott of the city’s buses that lasted 381 days. The economic impact was significant: African Americans made up about 75% of bus passengers. A young Baptist minister, Martin Luther King Jr, emerged as the spokesman for the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA). His oratorical skill and philosophy of non-violent resistance made him a national figure. In November 1956, the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott had succeeded.

Three organisations shaped the early civil rights movement. The SCLC — Southern Christian Leadership Conference — was founded in 1957 by King and other Black ministers. It used the Black church network as its organisational base and King’s philosophy of non-violent direct action as its method. The NAACP continued its legal work and lobbying. In April 1960, younger activists — many inspired by the Greensboro sit-ins of February 1960, when four Black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter at Woolworth’s — founded the SNCC (Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee). Ella Baker, who had worked for both the NAACP and SCLC, helped organise the founding meeting and encouraged the student activists to maintain their independence.

The Role of Emmett Till

Before the Montgomery boycott, a single murder illustrated the extreme violence underpinning Southern segregation. In August 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black teenager from Chicago visiting relatives in Mississippi, was abducted, tortured and murdered by two white men who claimed he had ‘offended’ a white woman. His killers were acquitted by an all-white jury in 67 minutes. Till’s mother, Mamie Till, insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of his body were published in Jet magazine and shocked Black America. Rosa Parks later said that when she refused to give up her seat, she was thinking of Emmett Till.

King drew on the teachings of Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi as well as the Sermon on the Mount. He argued that non-violent direct action accomplished two things simultaneously: it demonstrated the moral superiority of the civil rights movement by refusing to respond to violence with violence; and it forced authorities into a position where, if they used violence against peaceful protesters, they would reveal their own brutality to a watching nation. This tactic would reach its fullest expression in Birmingham in 1963. Examiners will reward students who understand that non-violence was a deliberate strategic choice as well as a moral one, not simply a passive response.

Key Fact

Rosa Parks was a trained NAACP activist, not simply a tired worker who refused to move. Her arrest in December 1955 was used as a deliberate legal test case because she was a composed, respectable plaintiff whose case would attract maximum public support.
exam_tip_html: Examiners reward complexity on Rosa Parks — make clear she was a trained NAACP activist, not just a ‘tired seamstress.’ On Little Rock, show you understand Eisenhower’s reluctance but explain why he had to act (federal authority). When explaining the SCLC, SNCC and NAACP, focus on what made each one distinctive rather than listing them. In a question about King’s leadership, explain why non-violent direct action worked as a tactic, not just that it was his approach. Dates matter: boycott began 1 December 1955 and ended in victory November 1956; Greensboro sit-ins February 1960; SNCC April 1960.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 381-day Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56), triggered by Rosa Parks’ deliberate arrest, demonstrated the economic power of collective Black action and launched Martin Luther King Jr as a national civil rights leader.
  • Little Rock (1957) showed that Brown required federal enforcement: Eisenhower sent troops not out of enthusiasm for civil rights but because state defiance of federal authority had to be confronted.
  • Three organisations — the NAACP (legal), the SCLC (church-based non-violent protest) and SNCC (student grassroots activism) — provided the movement’s organisational backbone by 1960.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955–1956.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Identifies a specific feature with detail, e.g. the boycott lasted 381 days and African Americans, who made up about 75% of bus passengers, stayed off the buses, causing serious economic damage to the bus company. Secure: Correct identification with some detail. Developing: Vague reference to the boycott. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the roles played by civil rights organisations in the movement between 1954 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) the NAACP used court cases like Brown v Board to overturn segregation laws; (2) the SCLC, founded by King in 1957, used the Black church network to coordinate non-violent direct action campaigns. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Martin Luther King Jr emerged as the leading figure of the civil rights movement between 1955 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple reasons with specific evidence — his oratorical skill demonstrated at the MIA meetings; his philosophy of non-violent direct action gave the movement a coherent and effective strategy; the Montgomery boycott provided a high-profile success to build on; SCLC gave him an organisational base. Shows how these factors combined. Secure: Two or more reasons with evidence. Developing: Describes King without explaining why he rose to leadership. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Little Rock crisis of 1957 was a significant moment in the civil rights movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons, e.g. (1) it demonstrated that the federal government would use military force to uphold Brown, setting a precedent for future federal intervention; (2) images of soldiers escorting nine children past jeering crowds were seen globally, exposing Southern resistance to an international audience during the Cold War. Each reason includes specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with relevant evidence and explanation. Developing: Two reasons without clear development. Emerging: One weak point.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of Rosa Parks in the development of the civil rights movement?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis — significant because her arrest sparked the 381-day boycott that proved Black economic power and launched King; her status as an NAACP activist made her a carefully chosen catalyst. But places her significance in context: Brown had created the legal framework; the NAACP had planned the campaign; she was one part of a coordinated strategy. Compares her significance to King, the NAACP, and the movement as a whole. Integrated judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence. Developing: Describes Parks without weighing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the developments in the civil rights movement between 1954 and 1960.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering Brown's ruling and resistance (Little Rock 1957), the Montgomery boycott (Parks, King, Browder v Gayle), the role of organisations (NAACP, SCLC, SNCC), Greensboro sit-ins, and Emmett Till's galvanising effect. Reaches an integrated judgement about what was achieved and what remained undone by 1960. Well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several developments with evidence and some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes events in chronological order with limited analysis. Emerging: Brief narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: How long did the Montgomery Bus Boycott last?
Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock in 1957?
options: Because he was a strong supporter of civil rights
Because the governor had defied a federal court order
Because the SCLC requested federal intervention
Because Brown v Board required immediate desegregation

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Rosa Parks strategically chosen by the NAACP?
flashcard_questions.a: She was a trained activist and a composed, credible plaintiff, unlike earlier potential test cases.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Montgomery Bus Boycott end, and how?
flashcard_questions.a: November 1956, when the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Little Rock Nine do in 1957?
flashcard_questions.a: Attempted to enrol at Central High School, Little Rock, facing National Guard and violent mob opposition.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Emmett Till significant to the civil rights movement?
flashcard_questions.a: His open-casket funeral in 1955 showed the brutal reality of racial violence, galvanising Black America.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the SCLC founded, and by whom?
flashcard_questions.a: 1957, by Martin Luther King Jr and other Black ministers.
February 1960: four Black students sat at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter, triggering a wave of similar protests.

flashcard_questions.q: What was King's philosophy of protest?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-violent direct action — forcing authorities to reveal their brutality to a watching nation without resorting to violence.

glossary_terms.definition: The nine African American students who attempted to enrol at the all-white Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, in September 1957, facing violent opposition.
Civil rights activist who in December 1955 refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, triggering the 381-day bus boycott.
Civil rights leader and Baptist minister who led the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the SCLC, advocating non-violent direct action and becoming the movement's most prominent public voice.
The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded by King and others in 1957, which coordinated civil rights campaigns across the South using Black churches as its organisational base.
The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, founded in 1960, which brought younger, more grassroots-based activists into the civil rights movement and would later develop a more radical direction.
